outcomes.absoluteFailure:
Among the tales handed down in the Vales of Anduin, some trace the existence of the great black wolves to an ancient practice of the Orcs of the mountains. Deep within the remotest dens, the Orcs are said to have discovered a strain of wolves whose cubs grow far more swiftly than those of other packs. They seize them at birth, feed them plentifully and subject them to cruel training until they are able to bear warriors upon their backs. The largest become the mounts of chieftains, while the others are taught to follow trails and pursue the enemies of the Orcs. According to this tradition, their ferocity springs from the ill-treatment they endure and from the habit of killing instilled in them by their masters.

The elders also say that, beneath their fearsome appearance, these animals retain the ordinary instincts of wolves. They acknowledge the authority of the strongest and may be brought to heel by one who succeeds in overcoming them without killing them. Some hunters even believe that the mere presence of a man capable of taking the shape of a bear is enough to inspire lasting submission in them, so greatly do they fear the mighty beasts of the forests. A Warg separated from its riders and raised far from the Orcs would thus eventually recover the ways of a wild animal, and might be taught to guard a dwelling or accompany a herd. The malice attributed to it would be chiefly a lingering consequence of the masters to whom it once belonged.
outcomes.failure:
The men of the vales know of the great wolves that sometimes come down from the mountains in the company of Orc-bands. Their accounts describe powerful beasts, able to cover great distances, recover an old trail and move through woodland with remarkable stealth. Hunters know that their presence may be betrayed by unusually large footprints and by howls unlike those of ordinary wolves. Wargs often gather in substantial packs, and some are sturdy enough to carry an Orc warrior. Families living near the paths used by such bands retain the memory of their attacks upon livestock and travellers.

You also know a tradition according to which the Orcs command their Wargs through a language of cries and growls. The animals are said to have learnt to recognise these sounds during their training, while their own howls enable them to relay a rider's orders throughout the pack. Hunters who offer this explanation point out that their coordinated attacks almost invariably appear to be directed by a leader, generally mounted upon the largest beast. They therefore conclude that a pack deprived of this guide loses its cohesion and soon scatters. Some guardians of the mountain passes consequently believe that the surest defence is to bring down the riders first, then allow the creatures, bereft of command, to withdraw of their own accord.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
The traditions of the Beornings distinguish Wargs from the wolves that naturally inhabit the mountains and forests. These great canids possess considerable strength, a keen sense of smell and hearing capable of detecting the slightest movement. Some are large enough to bear an Orc warrior, and their long strides make them dangerous pursuers of travellers attempting to escape on foot. Hunters' accounts describe them as tenacious trackers, able to recognise signs of passage and cross difficult ground. Their presence is especially feared when several individuals move together.

You also know that Wargs understand far more than ordinary wolves. They communicate through howls and growls to which their fellows respond, and can act in concert without a rider directing their every movement. The Beornings know of their alliance with the Orcs, but distinguish the packs that accompany warriors from the mountains from those that roam the wild lands on their own account. The accounts passed down to young hunters dwell upon this intelligence: a Warg may temporarily abandon a pursuit, go around an obstacle or rejoin its companions before returning to its prey.
outcomes.success:
The Beornings preserve a detailed knowledge of Wargs, sustained by hunting tales, the watch kept over mountain passes and encounters with the servants of the Shadow. They know that these creatures possess a language of their own, through which they exchange warnings, gather their fellows and agree upon common courses of action. Their alliance with the Orcs rests upon shared interests and upon their hostility towards the peoples who dwell in the vales and wooded lands. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands to scout the paths, pursue fugitives or fall upon the flanks of a company. The packs retain their own leaders and can act independently of their allies.

The traditions of those who guard the vales attach great importance to the way in which Wargs conduct a hunt. They may separate while following a trail, seek favourable passages to outflank their adversaries and come together again as they approach an obstacle. Their cries enable several individuals to alter their movements without losing contact with the pack. They also recognise the strength of an organised defence and may postpone an attack until an opponent becomes isolated. Beornings familiar with these creatures know that howls heard at a distance may herald concerted movements, even when no Warg is yet in sight.

The memory of those who protect the passes also recalls that Wargs remain dangerous after an Orc-band has disappeared. A pack that loses its riders retains the ability to choose a route, recognise the tracks of its enemies and pursue an undertaking already begun. Its conduct depends upon its own decisions no less than upon the alliances it maintains.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The oldest traditions of the Beornings draw a careful distinction between natural wolves, Wargs and the other wolf-like creatures that serve the powers of the Shadow. Ordinary wolves hunt and live according to the necessities of their kind; Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to deliberate, form alliances and pursue designs of their own. The most respected accounts ascribe to them a malevolent will that is strengthened, but not wholly explained, by their association with the Orcs. Their collective organisation belongs to their own nature: they acknowledge their leaders, gather to decide upon an undertaking and may choose either to fight beside an Orc-band or to range the wild lands alone.

Those who guard the passes also know the differences between the habits of particular packs. Some occupy a valley or the approaches to a mountain for a considerable time; others follow the movements of Orc warriors and travel great distances in their company. Wargs recognise the routes taken by travellers, the places where a path narrows and the obstacles that hinder escape. Their coordination allows them to test a defence, spread out and concentrate their attack upon a less well-protected part of a company. A withdrawal may be the outcome of a collective decision, and a pack that appears to have scattered retains the means to gather swiftly again. Such behaviour explains the caution of experienced hunters when they discover several trails converging upon the same passage.

Certain Beorning traditions trace the appearance of these creatures back to the ancient corruption of living things by the powers of the Shadow. They tell of wolves whose nature was altered until they acquired a malice and an intelligence foreign to their original stock. Other accounts distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, to which Elven tales attribute a different spiritual nature. Beornings acquainted with these traditions know that outwardly similar great wolves may conceal beings of different kinds. Above all, they recognise Wargs by their language, their organisation and their ability to plan undertakings with the Orcs while preserving their independence.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — the claims that Wargs may be domesticated or made submissive to skin-changers are invented; failure — their coordination is wrongly attributed to Orcish command; successful results — their intelligence, language and independence are grounded in Tolkien. The particular beliefs presented in the two failed results are MERP-UI inventions.
